passage:
Monday: A fake account posted Chandrika's old photo with a cruel caption, and forty people laughed. Her hands shook. She typed a reply about the bully's family that she was sure would sting, her thumb over the button.
Tuesday: Amandeep found her by the water cooler. "Don't send it. They'll screenshot you and then you're the one in trouble." She didn't answer, but she deleted the draft, hot-faced. "I still want to hurt them," she admitted. "Of course you do," Amandeep said. "That's human." They gathered screenshots and dates instead.
The following Monday: They gave the file to the vice-principal, who took the account down and spoke to the students involved. Chandrika still felt anger sometimes, but she felt steadier.

qa.q: How many people laughed at the fake account's post?
What was Chandrika feeling when she typed the reply, and what did she admit on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was shaking with anger and wanted the reply to sting; on Tuesday she admitted she still wanted to hurt them.

qa.q: Why was gathering screenshots and dates a better choice than the reply?
qa.a: Evidence can be handed to the school to act on, while a cruel reply could be screenshotted and turn the trouble onto Chandrika herself.

qa.q: How might the vice-principal see Chandrika's file?
qa.a: The vice-principal would see clear evidence and a student who chose to report rather than retaliate, and can act on it fairly.

grounding: Shows a teen wanting to retaliate against a bully, recognising the urge, and choosing evidence and reporting.

passage:
Wednesday night

Zubin commented on my dance video in front of the whole class group: "Looks like a cow having a fit." Twenty people laughed. I read it in the bus and my face burned so hot I thought I'd cry right there.

I got home and I was SO angry. I have an old photo of Zubin from Class 7 when he fell in the mud at the picnic. I opened it. I typed a caption. I wanted him to feel exactly what I felt. My thumb was on post.

Then I thought: then it's two people being cruel. And he'll hit back, and it'll go on for weeks, and maybe I'll be the one in trouble.

I deleted it. My hands were still shaking.

Instead I screenshotted his comment and the laughing replies. I showed Mumma. She was quiet, then angry for me. She emailed my class teacher right then, with the screenshots, and said we'll talk to the school tomorrow.

I still want revenge a little. But I'm glad I didn't.

Sunaina

qa.q: What did Zubin comment on the dance video?
qa.a: Zubin commented, "Looks like a cow having a fit."

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when the thumb was on post?
qa.a: Sunaina felt furious and humiliated, wanting Zubin to feel the same hurt.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than revenge, and why?
qa.a: Saving screenshots and showing Mumma worked better, because it stopped the cruelty spiralling and got the school involved.

qa.q: How did Mumma react to the screenshots?
qa.a: Mumma was quiet, then angry on Sunaina's behalf, and emailed the class teacher at once.

grounding: It shows a teen tempted to hit back at a cyberbully with something equally cruel, recognising the impulse and choosing evidence and reporting instead.

Damini deleted the diary photos from her phone. She went to the living room with the screenshots. Her father read them carefully, then said, "This isn't okay. Thank you for not hitting back." He emailed the principal that night and asked for a meeting first thing.

qa.q: What did Tanvi do to Damini's photo?
qa.a: Tanvi edited Damini's photo and sent it round the whole batch.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she messaged Vijay?
qa.a: Damini felt furious and humiliated, shaking with anger and wanting to hurt Tanvi back.

qa.q: Why did Vijay urge evidence and reporting instead of revenge?
qa.a: Vijay knew posting the diary would get Damini into trouble too and keep the fight going, while evidence and reporting would get adults to act.

qa.q: How did Damini's father respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: He said it wasn't okay, thanked her for not hitting back and emailed the principal that night, so Damini felt supported.

grounding: It shows a teen who wants to hit back at cyberbullying with something equally cruel, and chooses evidence and reporting, with a parent acting that night.
